record.paper_title: Open Problems within Nonextensive Statistical Mechanics
record.original_question: Does the shape parameter, also called nonlinear statistical coupling, provide a quantification of a system’s statistical complexity? Can this definition of statistical complexity be related to other kinds of complexity, such as algorithmic complexity, and can statistical complexity be explained through its inverse, the statistical degrees of freedom?

evidence.quote: The coupling term is not new, in fact, it has a long tradition within statistical analysis as the shape parameter defining the deviation from exponential decay and it is the inverse of the degrees of freedom used to define the Student’s t distribution. And so, the final open problem for the reader to consider is whether the coupling or shape parameter is an appropriate measure of a system’s statistical complexity.

Open Problem 7: Does the shape parameter also referred to as the nonlinear statistical coupling provide a quantification of a system’s statistical complexity? Can this definition of statistical complexity be related to other forms of complexity, such as algorithmic complexity? Explain the statistical complexity in terms of its inverse the statistical degrees of freedom.

Define a measure of statistical complexity. The author has proposed that the nonlinear statistical coupling, which is equal to the shape parameter and the inverse of the degrees of freedom, is a measure of statistical complexity.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider heavy-tailed probability distributions of generalized-Pareto / Student's t type. For a real parameter κ ≥ 0 (the "nonlinear statistical coupling," equal to the shape parameter governing the deviation from exponential decay in such heavy-tailed families and equal to the reciprocal 1/ν of the degrees-of-freedom parameter ν of the Student's t distribution), the generalized exponential is defined by exp_κ(x) = (1 + κ x)_+^{1/κ} (with exp_0(x) = e^x), and the associated coupled (Tsallis-type) distributions have density proportional to exp_κ(−β|x|^a) for suitable a, β > 0.

(a) Determine whether κ provides a quantitative measure of the statistical complexity of a system described by such a distribution; i.e., construct (or rule out) a rigorous notion of "statistical complexity" C(P) of a probability distribution P with the property that C is a monotone function of κ on the family of coupled distributions and that satisfies natural axioms expected of a complexity measure (e.g., vanishing for both deterministic and maximally random limits, invariance properties, additivity behaviour).

(b) If such a measure exists, establish a precise relationship between this statistical complexity and algorithmic (Kolmogorov) complexity of typical samples drawn from the distribution.

(c) Provide an interpretation of this statistical complexity in terms of its reciprocal 1/κ, the "statistical degrees of freedom," making explicit how growth of degrees of freedom corresponds to decrease of complexity and recovers, in the limit 1/κ → ∞, the exponential (Gaussian-type) case of minimal coupling.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open conceptual/foundational question in nonextensive statistical mechanics. No definitive resolution—i.e., a rigorous, widely-accepted axiomatic equivalence between the nonlinear statistical coupling and a measure of statistical complexity, with a proven link to algorithmic complexity—appears in the literature. Related complexity measures (LMC, statistical complexity of López-Ruiz–Mancini–Calbet, Tsallis-entropy-based complexity) exist but do not constitute a resolution of this specific question.
